summary: Defines the vCard data format for representing and exchanging information about people and other entities, such as names, addresses, email, phone numbers, photos, and logos. It replaced RFCs 2425, 2426, and 4770 and updated RFC 2739.

plainLanguage.summary: A vCard is a digital business card. This defines a common file format so contact details can move between phones, email programs, and address books.

questions: how do vcard lines get folded
subtitle: The text format that lets address books, phones and mail programs swap contact cards.

tldr.problem: Address books are on many kinds of devices and platforms, and they need a common way to capture and exchange contact data.
tldr.mechanism: vCard 4.0 is a UTF-8 text format. Each card is a BEGIN:VCARD to END:VCARD block of lines, and each line is a property such as FN, TEL or EMAIL, optionally with parameters like PREF or TYPE.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6350 obsoletes RFCs 2425, 2426 and 4770 and updates RFC 2739. It is a Proposed Standard, and RFC 6868, RFC 9554 and RFC 9555 update it.

today: RFC 6350 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 6868, RFC 9554 and RFC 9555. It obsoletes RFC 2425, RFC 2426 and RFC 4770 and updates RFC 2739.

sections.title: Why a Common Contact Format
sections.content:
Electronic address books are everywhere, including on portable, connected devices, and many different platforms exchange contact data. vCard is the format that lets them capture and exchange the information normally kept in an address book or directory application.

The data travels as the text/vcard MIME content type, usually describing one contact or a group of contacts. This RFC merges the older RFC 2425 and RFC 2426, folds in the IMPP property from RFC 4770 and the calendar properties of RFC 2739, and makes vCard a stand-alone format rather than only a MIME type.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone keeps friends' phone numbers somewhere. vCard is a shared way to write them down so any phone can read what another phone wrote.

sections.title: Lines, Folding and Escaping
sections.content:
The character set is always UTF-8, and there is no way to override it. Lines end in a CRLF. A vCard starts with BEGIN:VCARD, must have VERSION:4.0 immediately after, and ends with END:VCARD. It MUST include the VERSION and FN properties.

Each content line is an optional group, a property name, optional ;-separated parameters, a colon and a value. Names are case-insensitive, though upper case is RECOMMENDED on output. Long lines SHOULD be folded to at most 75 octets by inserting a CRLF followed by a single space or tab. Unfolding removes the CRLF and that one white space character.

Escaping is strict. A comma in a value MUST be escaped with a backslash. A semicolon inside a field of a compound property such as N or ADR MUST be escaped. A backslash is written as two backslashes, and a newline is written as a backslash followed by n or N. Escaping MUST NOT be used in other cases.
sections.plainLanguage: A vCard is a list of labelled lines, like a form with one answer per line. If a line is too long you may break it, as long as the next piece starts with a space.

sections.title: Value Types and Parameters
sections.content:
Each property has a value type. The standard ones are text, uri, date, time, date-time, date-and-or-time, timestamp, boolean, integer, float, utc-offset and language-tag. Dates and times use only the basic format of ISO 8601, so a birthday may be 19850412, 1985-04 or the truncated --0412. Integers are limited to a signed 64-bit range.

Parameters add meta-information to a property. The RFC defines LANGUAGE, VALUE, PREF, ALTID, PID, TYPE, MEDIATYPE, CALSCALE, SORT-AS, GEO and TZ. PREF is an integer from 1 to 100, where 1 is most preferred. ALTID tags several property instances as alternative representations of one logical property, such as a name in two languages, and those instances count once toward cardinality.

Applications MUST ignore x-param and iana-param values they do not recognize.
sections.plainLanguage: Each line says what kind of answer it holds, like a date or a web address. Little tags such as 'preferred' or 'work' can be stuck on a line to say more about it.

sections.title: The vCard Properties
sections.content:
Section 6 lists the standard properties in groups. General: BEGIN, END, SOURCE, KIND and XML. Identification: FN, N, NICKNAME, PHOTO, BDAY, ANNIVERSARY and GENDER. Also ADR for delivery addresses, and TEL, EMAIL, IMPP and LANG for communications, TZ and GEO for geography, and TITLE, ROLE, LOGO, ORG, MEMBER and RELATED for organizations.

FN (the formatted name) is the one property that MUST appear. N is structured: family names, given names, additional names, honorific prefixes and honorific suffixes, separated by semicolons. ADR has seven positional components, from post office box to country name, and the first two (post office box and extended address) SHOULD be empty because they cause interoperability problems.

KIND says what the card represents: individual (the default), group, org or location. An org card MUST NOT contain MEMBER properties. TEL values SHOULD be URIs, expected to use the tel scheme, with TYPE values such as voice, fax, cell, video, pager, text and textphone.

Further properties include CATEGORIES, NOTE, PRODID, REV, SOUND, UID, URL, VERSION, KEY for cryptographic keys, FBURL, CALADRURI and CALURI. Private properties with names starting X- may be agreed bilaterally, and new ones are registered with IANA.

Properties with cardinality *1 (at most one) cannot carry a PID parameter, and CLIENTPIDMAP is the one property that cannot carry PID at all.
sections.plainLanguage: A card can hold many kinds of facts: name, phone, email, address, a photo, and even whether the card is for a person, a company or a place. Only the display name is required.

sections.title: Synchronization Between Devices
sections.content:
vCard data is often copied between devices, so version 4.0 adds two matching mechanisms. The UID property identifies a whole vCard, and vCards with equivalent UIDs MUST be matched. The PID parameter identifies one property instance among several, for example one of a person's email addresses.

A PID value is a local number, optionally followed by a dot and a source identifier. The CLIENTPIDMAP property gives each source identifier a global meaning by mapping it to a URI, for which the RFC says a urn:uuid is well suited. Two PIDs match when their local values are equal and their source identifiers map to equivalent URIs. Properties with different names MUST NOT be matched, and properties with a maximum cardinality of 1 MUST be matched.

In all other cases, matching is at the discretion of the synchronization engine. The RFC's worked example has two devices add different emails and phone numbers at once. The emails are kept as separate entries, while a smart engine merges the two matching phone numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: If two phones each have a copy of the same card and both change it, the cards carry little ID stickers. The stickers let the phones tell which lines are the same and which are new.

sections.title: Security and Privacy of Cards
sections.content:
vCards have no authentication or confidentiality of their own. They often hold sensitive data such as birthdays, addresses and phone numbers, and they are often carried by Internet mail, which is subject to monitoring, replay and forgery. Where confidentiality or authenticity matters, the vCard SHOULD be transported using a mechanism such as S/MIME or OpenPGP. The KEY property can carry the public key those mechanisms use.

Information in a card can go out of date. An originator who cares about freshness SHOULD specify SOURCE, and REV can record the last update time. Many properties carry URIs, so the URI security considerations of RFC 3986 apply.
sections.plainLanguage: A card has your address and phone number on it and no lock. If it is private, send it in a locked envelope.

sections.title: Media Type and Registries
sections.content:
IANA registered the text/vcard media type, with file extensions .vcf and .vcard, and marked text/directory as deprecated. The older text/x-vcard is also considered deprecated. The optional version parameter must agree with every card's VERSION property, and only UTF-8 may be used as the charset.

The RFC also creates registries for vCard properties, parameters, value data types and values. New elements are reviewed by a designated expert on the vcarddav@ietf.org list and published in an RFC, and changing an element from a Standards Track RFC requires a Standards Track RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: There is an official list of the kinds of lines a card can have. If you want a new kind, you have to ask the list keepers and write it down publicly.

data.title: A vCard for a person
data.code:
BEGIN:VCARD
VERSION:4.0
KIND:individual
FN:Jane Doe
ORG:ABC\, Inc.;North American Division;Marketing
END:VCARD

items.label: A group of persons or entities
items.desc: Usually has MEMBER properties, though not required.

items.label: An organization
items.desc: A single entity that is not a person; MUST NOT contain MEMBER.

items.label: A named geographical place
items.desc: Usually has a GEO property, though not required.
